note: Cardiology progress dictation, hospital day 2, on a 54-year-old male admitted for evaluation of palpitations. He came in two days ago after several weeks of episodes where his heart feels like it is racing and fluttering, lasting about ten to twenty minutes and mostly happening in the evening after coffee. He denies chest pain, denies syncope, denies shortness of breath, and denies any lightheadedness during the episodes. He is very anxious about all of this and has asked me many questions this morning, including whether this could be a heart attack, whether he will need a pacemaker, and whether he can keep drinking coffee, and I answered each of them at the bedside. Past history includes hypertension and generalized anxiety disorder, and at home he takes lisinopril 10 mg daily and sertraline 50 mg daily, with no known drug allergies. On telemetry overnight he had two short runs of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, the longest about four minutes with a rate up to 128, and otherwise sinus rhythm. Vitals this morning are blood pressure 146 over 88, heart rate 82, respiratory rate 16, temperature 36.9 Celsius, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. On exam he is anxious but comfortable, the rhythm is regular at the moment with no murmurs, the lungs are clear, there is no leg edema, and the thyroid is not enlarged. Troponin was negative twice, potassium 4.2, magnesium 2.0, TSH 1.8, and hemoglobin 14.6. The ECG on admission showed normal sinus rhythm without ST changes, and the echocardiogram this morning shows an ejection fraction of 60 percent, normal chamber sizes, and no significant valve disease. My impression is new paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 1 for hypertension, plus hypertension above goal and anxiety that is likely contributing to his symptoms. Plan is to start metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily for rate control, correction, make that 50 mg daily, to increase lisinopril from 10 mg to 20 mg daily, to continue sertraline, to stop caffeine, and to place a 14 day ambulatory event monitor at discharge. We discussed anticoagulation, and given the score of 1 we will review it in clinic rather than start it now. He will follow up with cardiology in two weeks. I spent extra time reassuring him and he says he feels better.
summary: A 54-year-old male was admitted for evaluation of palpitations, with several weeks of racing, fluttering episodes lasting ten to twenty minutes and no chest pain, syncope, shortness of breath or lightheadedness. He is very anxious and asked many questions, which were answered at the bedside. Telemetry showed brief runs of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, while troponin, potassium, magnesium, TSH, ECG and echocardiogram were normal or negative and blood pressure was 146 over 88. The impression is new paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with hypertension above goal and contributing anxiety. Metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily is started, lisinopril is increased to 20 mg daily, sertraline continues, caffeine is stopped, and a 14 day ambulatory event monitor with cardiology follow-up in two weeks is planned.

note:
Doctor: Hello, I'm the emergency physician. I understand you're an 84-year-old male with chest pain. Tell me what happened.
Patient: It started about two hours ago while I was watching television. It's a pressure right in the middle of my chest. Is this a heart attack? Should I be scared?
Doctor: We are going to find out, and we are moving quickly. Does the pain travel anywhere, like your arm or your jaw?
Patient: A little bit down my left arm. What tests are you going to do? Will they hurt?
Doctor: Just a blood draw and an ECG, nothing painful. Have you had any shortness of breath, nausea, or vomiting?
Patient: No shortness of breath and no vomiting. I felt a little sweaty when it started. Why would I be sweaty?
Doctor: That can happen with heart pain. Any cough, fever, or leg swelling?
Patient: No cough, no fever, and no swelling in my legs.
Doctor: What medical conditions do you have?
Patient: High blood pressure and high cholesterol, and I had a stent placed in my heart about six years ago. Does that matter?
Doctor: It matters a lot, thank you for telling me. What medicines do you take?
Patient: Aspirin 81 milligrams every morning, atorvastatin 40 milligrams at night, and lisinopril 20 milligrams in the morning. I took my aspirin today already. Is that okay?
Doctor: Yes, that's good. Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: None that I know of.
Doctor: Your blood pressure is 158 over 92, heart rate 88, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and temperature 36.7 Celsius. Your lungs are clear, your heart sounds are normal with no murmur, your chest wall is not tender, and there is no swelling in your legs. Your ECG shows a normal rhythm with no ST elevation and no new changes compared with your old tracing. Your first troponin is negative.
Patient: So it's not a heart attack?
Doctor: Not so far, but one troponin is not enough, so we will repeat it in three hours. My working diagnosis is unstable angina in a man with known coronary artery disease and a stent, and we need to rule out an acute coronary syndrome. I am giving you nitroglycerin 0.4 mg under your tongue now, and I want to increase your atorvastatin from 40 mg to 80 mg nightly. We will also get a chest x-ray, call the cardiologist, and admit you to the hospital on a heart monitor. If the repeat troponin stays negative, you will likely have a stress test tomorrow.
Patient: How long will I be here? Can someone call my doctor?
Doctor: Probably overnight, and yes, we will let your primary doctor know.
summary: An 84-year-old male presented to the emergency department with two hours of central chest pressure going a little down the left arm, with some initial sweatiness and no shortness of breath, vomiting, cough, fever or leg swelling. He has high blood pressure, high cholesterol and a prior stent, and he was anxious and asked many questions. The ECG showed no ST elevation or new changes and the first troponin was negative. The working diagnosis is unstable angina, with acute coronary syndrome to be ruled out. He received nitroglycerin, atorvastatin was increased to 80 mg nightly, and a repeat troponin, chest x-ray, cardiology call and admission on a heart monitor were planned.

First troponin is negative.

note:
Hospital day 2 for a 65-year-old male admitted with acute kidney injury from dehydration. He presented with four days of poor oral intake, nausea, and several loose stools, and he felt weak and dizzy when standing at home. He lives alone and has limited social support, with no family nearby, and he says it was hard to get out to buy food and drinks during the past week. He denies fever, chest pain, blood in the stool, and flank pain. His history includes hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Home medications were lisinopril 20 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, and metformin 1000 mg twice daily, and all three were held on admission. He has no known drug allergies.

Overnight there were no acute events. He received 2 liters of lactated Ringer's yesterday and is now on maintenance fluids at 100 mL per hour, and he has been drinking more this morning. He says the dizziness on standing has resolved and the nausea is gone. Vitals this morning are BP 128/76, HR 78, RR 16, temp 36.8 Celsius, and SpO2 97% on room air. On exam his mucous membranes are now moist, the heart rhythm is regular, the lungs are clear, the abdomen is soft and nontender, and there is no leg edema. Creatinine was 2.4 on admission, compared with a baseline of 1.0, and it is 1.6 today. BUN has improved from 42 to 28, potassium is 4.4 after 4.9 on admission, and sodium is 136. Urinalysis showed no protein or blood, and the renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis.

The kidney injury is prerenal from dehydration, made worse by lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide, and it is improving with fluids. Plan is to continue IV fluids until he is drinking well and then stop them, to keep holding lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, and metformin, to check fingerstick glucose before meals while metformin is held, and to repeat a basic metabolic panel in the morning. Because he lives alone, I have asked social work and case management to arrange home health, meal delivery, and a follow-up phone call after discharge, and physical therapy will evaluate him before he leaves. He will see his primary care doctor within one week for a repeat basic metabolic panel, and the home medications will be restarted gradually based on that result. He understands the plan.
summary: A 65-year-old male with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus was admitted with acute kidney injury from dehydration after four days of poor oral intake, nausea and loose stools. He lives alone with limited social support. On hospital day 2 his dizziness has resolved, vitals are normal, and creatinine has improved from 2.4 to 1.6 against a baseline of 1.0, with a bland urinalysis and no hydronephrosis on renal ultrasound. The assessment is prerenal kidney injury worsened by lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide. The plan is to continue IV fluids until he drinks well, keep holding lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide and metformin, repeat a basic metabolic panel, involve social work, case management and physical therapy, and arrange primary care follow-up within one week.

note:
Doctor: Hi, thanks for coming in today. I see you're a 15-year-old female with asthma, and you've been having more trouble breathing. Tell me what's been going on.
Patient: For about four days I've been coughing a lot, especially at night, and I get wheezy walking between classes. I woke up three nights this week coughing.
Doctor: Any fever, sore throat, or runny nose?
Patient: No fever and no sore throat. My nose is stuffy, but that's my allergies.
Doctor: Any chest pain, or trouble finishing a sentence when you're short of breath?
Patient: No chest pain. I can talk okay, but I get winded climbing the stairs.
Doctor: What do you use for your asthma right now?
Patient: I have albuterol, and I use it when I'm wheezy, about once a day. Actually, no, that's wrong, it's more like four times a day this week. And I take a controller inhaler, fluticasone 110 micrograms, one puff twice a day, but I forget it a lot. I also take montelukast, the 5 mg one. Oh wait, I just looked at the bottle in my bag, it's the 10 mg tablet, once at night.
Doctor: Okay, thanks for checking. Any side effects from the montelukast?
Patient: I've been having really bad dreams since I started it a couple of months ago.
Doctor: That's important to know. What other medicines do you take?
Patient: Cetirizine 10 mg every day for my allergies. I also have eczema, but I haven't needed any cream lately.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Do you smoke, vape, or use any tobacco? This stays between us unless there is a safety issue.
Patient: I smoke about five cigarettes a day. I started vaping last year and switched to cigarettes a few months ago. I know it makes my breathing worse.
Doctor: Thank you for being honest with me. Have you ever been to the ED or hospital for your asthma?
Patient: Once, when I was twelve, I stayed overnight.
Doctor: Okay, let me tell you what I found. Your temperature is 37.0 Celsius, heart rate 98, respiratory rate 22, and SpO2 95% on room air. I hear wheezing throughout both lungs when you breathe out, and breathing out takes longer than normal, but you are not using your neck muscles and air is moving well. The lining of your nose looks pale and swollen. Your peak flow today is 280, which is about 70% of your personal best. The chest x-ray we took this morning shows hyperinflation and no pneumonia. After four puffs of albuterol through a spacer here, your peak flow went up to 340, the wheezing is much lighter, and your SpO2 is 98%.
Patient: So what is going on?
Doctor: You have a moderate asthma exacerbation. Your tobacco use and your allergic rhinitis are both making it worse, and we also know about your eczema. Here is the plan. I am starting prednisone 40 mg once a day for five days. Use albuterol, four puffs with the spacer, every four hours for the next two days, then only as needed. I want you to increase the fluticasone 110 micrograms to two puffs twice a day, and rinse your mouth afterward. Because of the bad dreams, I am stopping the montelukast. Keep taking the cetirizine 10 mg every day. I also want you to quit smoking. I will refer you to a teen quit program and give you a quitline number. We will repeat spirometry at a follow-up visit in one week, and I am giving you a written asthma action plan. Go to the ED if you need albuterol more often than every four hours or you cannot speak in full sentences.
Patient: Okay. Can I still do cross-country practice?
Doctor: Not until you are back to normal, and we will recheck you in a week.
summary: A 15-year-old female with asthma, allergic rhinitis and eczema presented with four days of cough, night waking and wheezing, with no fever, sore throat or chest pain. She disclosed smoking about five cigarettes a day and reported frequent albuterol use, missed controller doses and bad dreams on montelukast. Exam showed diffuse expiratory wheezing, SpO2 95% on room air and a peak flow of 280, with hyperinflation and no pneumonia on chest x-ray, and she improved after albuterol. The assessment is a moderate asthma exacerbation worsened by tobacco use and allergic rhinitis. Prednisone 40 mg daily for five days is started, fluticasone is increased, montelukast is stopped, and tobacco cessation support, an action plan and one-week follow-up with spirometry are arranged.

soap.subjective: 15-year-old female with asthma, allergic rhinitis and eczema. Four days of heavy coughing, worse at night, with wheezing walking between classes, three night wakings this week and feeling winded on stairs. Nose stuffy. Denies fever, sore throat and chest pain. Albuterol use rose from about once a day to about four times a day this week; fluticasone 110 micrograms one puff twice a day with frequently missed doses; montelukast 10 mg once at night, initially misreported as 5 mg, with bad dreams since starting; cetirizine 10 mg every day. No medication allergies. Smokes about five cigarettes a day after earlier vaping. One overnight hospital stay for asthma at age twelve.
soap.objective: Temperature 37.0 Celsius, heart rate 98, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 95% on room air. Wheezing throughout both lungs with prolonged expiration, no neck muscle use, good air movement, pale swollen nasal lining. Peak flow 280, about 70% of personal best. Chest x-ray shows hyperinflation without pneumonia. After four puffs of albuterol by spacer, peak flow 340, wheezing much lighter and SpO2 98%.
soap.assessment: Moderate asthma exacerbation worsened by tobacco use and allergic rhinitis, with eczema also noted.
plan: Start prednisone 40 mg once a day for five days
Albuterol four puffs with a spacer every four hours for two days, then as needed
Increase fluticasone 110 micrograms to two puffs twice a day and rinse the mouth afterward
Stop montelukast because of bad dreams
Continue cetirizine 10 mg every day
Advise quitting smoking, refer to a teen quit program and give a quitline number
Written asthma action plan
Repeat spirometry at a follow-up visit in one week
Go to the ED if albuterol is needed more often than every four hours or she cannot speak in full sentences

note:
Doctor: Good afternoon. You're a 54-year-old male here for follow-up of your systemic lupus erythematosus, correct? I know you couldn't get into your rheumatologist's office this week, so let's go over how you're doing.
Patient: Yes, that's right. My hands and wrists have been aching for about three weeks, mostly in the morning, and I've been very tired.
Doctor: How long does the morning stiffness last?
Patient: About thirty to forty minutes.
Doctor: Any rash on your face, or sores in your mouth?
Patient: No rash and no mouth sores. I do get a little sun sensitivity on my arms.
Doctor: Any fever, chest pain when you take a deep breath, or swelling in your legs?
Patient: No fever, no chest pain, and no leg swelling.
Doctor: Any foamy urine?
Patient: No, my urine looks normal.
Doctor: What medicines are you on?
Patient: Hydroxychloroquine 200 milligrams twice a day, prednisone 5 milligrams every morning, and amlodipine 5 milligrams for my blood pressure.
Doctor: Any medicine allergies?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Your blood pressure today is 136 over 84, heart rate 74, temperature 36.7 Celsius, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. On exam, several knuckles in both hands are tender with mild swelling and your wrists are tender, but there is no rash, no mouth ulcers, your lungs are clear, I hear no heart rub, and there is no swelling in your legs. Your labs from last week show a creatinine of 0.9, a urinalysis with no protein or blood, a mildly elevated anti-dsDNA, and a complement C3 that is slightly low at 82.
Patient: Is the lupus getting worse? Should I worry about my kidneys?
Doctor: Your kidney tests are reassuring. You have a mild lupus flare affecting your joints, and your hypertension is well controlled. Here is the plan. I am increasing your prednisone from 5 milligrams to 10 milligrams every morning for two weeks, and then we will taper it back down. Continue hydroxychloroquine 200 milligrams twice a day and amlodipine 5 milligrams. Please get a complete blood count, creatinine, urinalysis, and anti-dsDNA again in four weeks, and schedule your yearly eye exam because of the hydroxychloroquine. Use sunscreen and cover your arms outdoors. I will send my note to your rheumatologist, and please see them within two weeks.
Patient: Okay, that sounds good, thank you.
summary: A 54-year-old male with systemic lupus erythematosus was seen at urgent care for follow-up after about three weeks of aching hands and wrists with morning stiffness, fatigue and mild sun sensitivity, and he denies rash, mouth sores, fever, chest pain, leg swelling and foamy urine. Exam showed tender, mildly swollen knuckles and wrists, and recent labs showed a creatinine of 0.9, a urinalysis without protein or blood, a mildly elevated anti-dsDNA and a slightly low complement C3. The assessment is a mild lupus flare affecting the joints with well-controlled hypertension. Prednisone is increased to 10 mg every morning for two weeks, with repeat labs, an eye exam and rheumatology follow-up.

soap.subjective: 54-year-old male with systemic lupus erythematosus here for follow-up because he could not see his rheumatologist this week. About three weeks of aching hands and wrists, worse in the morning with stiffness lasting thirty to forty minutes, and he feels very tired. Mild sun sensitivity on the arms. Denies rash, mouth sores, fever, chest pain, leg swelling and foamy urine. Takes hydroxychloroquine 200 milligrams twice a day, prednisone 5 milligrams every morning and amlodipine 5 milligrams for blood pressure. No medicine allergies.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 136 over 84, heart rate 74, temperature 36.7 Celsius, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Several knuckles in both hands tender with mild swelling and tender wrists; no rash, no mouth ulcers, clear lungs, no heart rub, no leg swelling. Labs from last week: creatinine 0.9, urinalysis with no protein or blood, mildly elevated anti-dsDNA, complement C3 slightly low at 82.
soap.assessment: Mild lupus flare affecting the joints with reassuring kidney tests, and well-controlled hypertension.
plan: Increase prednisone from 5 milligrams to 10 milligrams every morning for two weeks, then taper back down
Continue hydroxychloroquine 200 milligrams twice a day and amlodipine 5 milligrams
Repeat complete blood count, creatinine, urinalysis and anti-dsDNA in four weeks

Use sunscreen and cover the arms outdoors
Send the note to the rheumatologist and see them within two weeks

note: Cardiology clinic dictation on an 85-year-old male seen for resistant hypertension. His blood pressure has stayed above goal for the past several months even though he says he takes his pills every day, and he brought a home log with readings mostly in the 160s over 80s. He denies headache, chest pain, shortness of breath, and dizziness on standing. He takes lisinopril 20 mg daily and amlodipine 10 mg daily, he reports he never misses a dose, and pill counts and pharmacy refill records confirm good adherence. He has no known drug allergies and no other chronic medical problems. In clinic his blood pressure is 168 over 86 in the right arm and 166 over 84 in the left arm, and his heart rate is 70 and regular. On exam the heart sounds are normal with no murmur, there are no carotid or abdominal bruits, the lungs are clear, and there is no leg edema. A basic metabolic panel last week showed potassium 4.3 and creatinine 1.1, and today's ECG shows sinus rhythm with mild left ventricular hypertrophy. My impression is resistant hypertension with no symptoms of end-organ damage. Plan is to increase lisinopril from 20 mg to 40 mg daily, to repeat the basic metabolic panel in two weeks, to order an aldosterone to renin ratio to screen for a secondary cause, and to have him keep a home blood pressure log. I will see him back in four weeks to decide about adding a third medication.
summary: An 85-year-old male was seen in cardiology clinic for resistant hypertension, with blood pressure above goal for several months despite confirmed adherence to lisinopril and amlodipine. He denies headache, chest pain, shortness of breath and dizziness on standing. Clinic blood pressure was 168 over 86 on the right and 166 over 84 on the left, the exam was unremarkable, and the ECG showed mild left ventricular hypertrophy, with potassium and creatinine recently normal. The impression is resistant hypertension. Lisinopril is increased to 40 mg daily, a basic metabolic panel will be repeated in two weeks, an aldosterone to renin ratio is ordered, and he will return in four weeks to consider a third medication.

Normal heart sounds without murmur, no carotid or abdominal bruits, clear lungs, no leg edema. Basic metabolic panel last week with potassium 4.3 and creatinine 1.1. ECG shows sinus rhythm with mild left ventricular hypertrophy.
soap.assessment: Resistant hypertension with no symptoms of end-organ damage.
plan: Increase lisinopril from 20 mg to 40 mg daily
Repeat the basic metabolic panel in two weeks
Order an aldosterone to renin ratio to screen for a secondary cause
Keep a home blood pressure log
Return in four weeks to decide about adding a third medication

note:
Follow-up visit in the psychiatry clinic for a 59-year-old male with generalized anxiety disorder. He works rotating shifts at a distribution center, alternating between day weeks and night weeks with little warning, and he says his anxiety and sleep have both been worse over the past two months. He describes near-constant worry about work performance, finances, and his health, along with muscle tension in the neck and shoulders, irritability, difficulty concentrating, and trouble falling asleep after night shifts. He denies suicidal thoughts, denies panic attacks, denies hallucinations, and denies any alcohol or drug use, although he drinks about five cups of coffee and one energy drink during a typical shift. GAD-7 today is 15, down from 17 at his last visit, and PHQ-9 is 7.

Medication history was reviewed in detail. He initially reported taking escitalopram 5 mg each day, but when he checked the pill bottle in his bag he clarified that the dose is 10 mg daily, which he takes whenever he wakes up, so the timing shifts by up to twelve hours depending on his schedule. He has also been using lorazepam 1 mg at bedtime about three nights per week to fall asleep, and he feels groggy the next morning. His other conditions are hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and GERD, treated with lisinopril 20 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, and omeprazole 20 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies.

On exam today he is alert and cooperative and appears tired, with good eye contact, normal speech, an anxious mood with congruent affect, a linear thought process, and no evidence of psychosis. Vitals are blood pressure 138/84 and heart rate 78. Labs from last week show sodium 139, creatinine 0.9, ALT 28, TSH 2.1, and hemoglobin A1c 6.8 percent. An ECG today shows a QTc of 420 ms.

My impression is that his generalized anxiety disorder is partially improved but still symptomatic, with insomnia driven largely by his shift schedule, while his hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and GERD are stable. I am increasing escitalopram from 10 mg to 20 mg daily, and I told him to take it at the same point in his waking day, whether that is morning or evening, rather than by the clock. I am stopping lorazepam because of next-day sedation, fall risk on night shifts, and the risk of dependence, and I am starting hydroxyzine 25 mg at bedtime as needed for sleep for the next month. He will continue lisinopril, metformin, and omeprazole unchanged. I am referring him for cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia and anxiety, and we agreed on a sleep plan with a fixed four hour anchor period of sleep every day, blackout curtains, and no caffeine in the second half of each shift. I offered a letter to his employer asking for a more predictable schedule, and he accepted. He will return in four weeks with a repeat sodium level, and he knows to call sooner if his mood worsens or he has thoughts of harming himself.
summary: A 59-year-old male shift worker with generalized anxiety disorder, hypertension, type 2 diabetes and GERD returned with worse anxiety and trouble falling asleep after night shifts, and he denies suicidal thoughts, panic attacks and hallucinations. GAD-7 is 15 and PHQ-9 is 7, and labs and ECG were unremarkable. He clarified that his current escitalopram dose is 10 mg daily, and he uses lorazepam about three nights a week with next-day grogginess. The impression is partially improved generalized anxiety disorder with shift-related insomnia. Escitalopram is increased to 20 mg daily, lorazepam is stopped, hydroxyzine 25 mg at bedtime as needed is started, and CBT referral, a sleep plan, an employer letter and four-week follow-up are arranged.

Blood pressure 138/84, heart rate 78. Labs from last week: sodium 139, creatinine 0.9, ALT 28, TSH 2.1, hemoglobin A1c 6.8 percent. ECG shows a QTc of 420 ms.

Stop lorazepam because of next-day sedation, fall risk and dependence risk
Start hydroxyzine 25 mg at bedtime as needed for sleep for the next month
Continue lisinopril, metformin and omeprazole unchanged
Refer for cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia and anxiety
Sleep plan with a fixed four hour anchor period of sleep every day, blackout curtains and no caffeine in the second half of each shift
Provide a letter to his employer asking for a more predictable schedule

note: Psychiatry consult dictation, hospital day 2, regarding a 65-year-old male on the medical ward who was admitted with chest tightness and palpitations and has had a negative cardiac workup. He describes repeated episodes with a pounding heart, sweating, shaking, chest tightness, shortness of breath, and a strong fear that he is dying. They come on suddenly for no clear reason and peak within about ten minutes. He has had four such attacks in the past month and now worries constantly about having another one. He denies suicidal thoughts, denies hallucinations, and denies alcohol or drug use. He has no other medical history, takes no regular medications, and has no known drug allergies. His troponin was negative twice, the ECG showed normal sinus rhythm, and the thyroid stimulating hormone was normal. On exam he is cooperative but visibly anxious, with a heart rate of 84, blood pressure 130 over 80, normal speech, linear thinking, and no evidence of psychosis. My impression is panic disorder. Plan is to start sertraline 25 mg daily, increasing to 50 mg daily after one week, to give lorazepam 0.5 mg once as needed for a severe attack during this admission only, to refer him for cognitive behavioral therapy, and to arrange psychiatry clinic follow-up in two weeks after discharge. I reviewed breathing techniques with him and explained that the attacks are not dangerous to his heart.
summary: A 65-year-old male on the medical ward, admitted with chest tightness and palpitations and a negative cardiac workup, was seen for recurrent attacks of pounding heart, sweating, shaking, chest tightness and shortness of breath with a fear of dying. He has had four attacks in the past month and denies suicidal thoughts, hallucinations and alcohol or drug use. Troponin, ECG and thyroid stimulating hormone were normal or negative, and he was anxious but cooperative with no psychosis. The impression is panic disorder. Sertraline 25 mg daily is started with a planned increase to 50 mg after one week, lorazepam 0.5 mg is available as needed during admission, and cognitive behavioral therapy and psychiatry follow-up in two weeks are arranged.

note:
Hospital day 3 for a 91-year-old female admitted with right lower-extremity cellulitis. She came in with three days of redness, warmth, and swelling of the right shin, along with chills at home, and she had a low-grade fever in the emergency department. She lives alone and has limited social support, with one neighbor who checks on her occasionally, and she waited several days before calling for help because she did not want to be a burden. Her history includes atrial fibrillation, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3, and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. On admission she gave her apixaban dose as 5 mg twice daily, but her neighbor brought in the pill bottles, and the pharmacy label and the pharmacy record both confirm that the correct dose is 2.5 mg twice daily, which is appropriate for her age and kidney function, so the 2.5 mg dose was ordered. She has no known drug allergies.

Her home medications are apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, linagliptin 5 mg daily, and furosemide 40 mg daily, and she takes acetaminophen as needed for joint pain. Vancomycin was started in the emergency department for possible MRSA, but there was no purulence, the nasal MRSA PCR was negative, and blood cultures show no growth at 48 hours, so I discontinued vancomycin yesterday and changed to cefazolin 1 gram IV every 8 hours. Furosemide was held on admission because of mild volume depletion and was resumed today at a lower dose of 20 mg daily.

She feels better today. The leg pain has improved, and she denies chest pain, shortness of breath, calf pain, and nausea. She was afebrile overnight. Vitals this morning are temperature 37.0 Celsius, HR 76 and irregular, BP 134/70, RR 18, and SpO2 96% on room air. On exam the erythema of the right shin has receded from the marked border by about 3 cm, there is mild warmth and tenderness, 1+ pitting edema, no fluctuance or purulence, and no crepitus, and the foot is warm with palpable pulses. The left leg is normal. White blood cell count was 14.2 on admission and 9.8 today, creatinine is 1.6 and near her baseline of 1.5, potassium is 4.3, and CRP has fallen from 86 to 40. A venous duplex of the right leg showed no deep vein thrombosis.

My impression is that the cellulitis is responding well to cefazolin. Her atrial fibrillation is rate controlled, her heart failure looks compensated, and her chronic kidney disease is at baseline. Plan is to continue cefazolin 1 gram IV every 8 hours for one more day and then switch to oral cephalexin 500 mg four times daily to finish a 7 day course, to elevate the leg and keep marking the border of the redness, to continue apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, amlodipine, and linagliptin, and to use acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain. Physical therapy and occupational therapy will evaluate her today. Because she lives alone with limited social support and now has reduced mobility, I have asked social work and case management to assess her for short-term skilled nursing facility rehab versus home with home health nursing, and to arrange meal delivery, a medical alert device, and pharmacy blister packs to prevent further dosing confusion. Discharge is anticipated in one to two days once a safe disposition is confirmed, with primary care follow-up within one week.

note:
Cardiology clinic visit for a 67-year-old female with peripheral artery disease who comes in for ongoing leg pain with walking. For about six months she has had cramping pain in both calves, worse on the right, that begins after she walks about two blocks and goes away within a few minutes of standing still. She denies pain at rest, denies foot ulcers or sores that are slow to heal, denies chest pain, and denies palpitations. She has hypertension and hyperlipidemia, and she takes amlodipine 5 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg daily. She has no known drug allergies. She currently smokes about half a pack of cigarettes per day and has done so for roughly 40 years, and she says she has tried to quit twice without success.

Vitals today are blood pressure 142/84 and heart rate 76. On exam the right dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are barely palpable and the left pulses are diminished, both feet are cool to the touch, and there are no ulcers, no gangrene, and capillary refill is under three seconds. Her ankle-brachial index today is 0.62 on the right and 0.78 on the left. Her LDL cholesterol last month was 128, and her hemoglobin A1c was 5.6 percent.

My impression is symptomatic peripheral artery disease with intermittent claudication, made worse by ongoing tobacco use and an LDL above goal. Plan is to start aspirin 81 mg daily, to increase atorvastatin from 20 mg to 80 mg daily, to begin a supervised exercise program with walking to near-maximal pain three times per week, and to order an arterial duplex ultrasound of both legs. We spent several minutes on smoking cessation, and since she is ready to try again I am starting a nicotine patch 14 mg daily and referring her to the state quitline. I explained that smoking is the most important modifiable factor for limb loss and heart attack. She should wear well-fitting shoes and check her feet every day. She will return in six weeks with a repeat lipid panel.
summary: A 67-year-old female with peripheral artery disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and current tobacco use has had six months of cramping calf pain after walking about two blocks, relieved by rest. She denies pain at rest, foot ulcers, chest pain and palpitations. Exam showed diminished pedal pulses with cool feet and no ulcers, and the ankle-brachial index was 0.62 on the right and 0.78 on the left, with an LDL of 128. The impression is symptomatic peripheral artery disease with intermittent claudication. Aspirin 81 mg daily and a nicotine patch are started, atorvastatin is increased to 80 mg daily, and a supervised exercise program, arterial duplex ultrasound, quitline referral and a six-week return with a lipid panel are planned.

note:
Urgent care visit, R shoulder injury.
26-year-old female c/o R shoulder pain x 4 days s/p fall onto outstretched R arm while snowboarding. Felt a "pop" at the time. Pain worse w/ overhead reaching and lifting, worse at night, hard to sleep on R side. Also c/o weakness lifting the arm. R hand dominant, works as a barista, worried about missing shifts. Tried ice and OTC pain meds w/ minimal relief.
Denies numbness, tingling, neck pain, fever, prior shoulder injury. No head strike, no LOC.
PMH: none. No surgeries. NKDA. No home meds.
Soc: smokes 1/2 ppd x 6 yrs, wants to quit, occ EtOH, no other drugs.

Exam: R shoulder no deformity, no ecchymosis, no effusion. Mild TTP ant/lateral shoulder. Active abduction limited to ~90 deg w/ pain, passive abduction full. + drop arm test. + empty can w/ supraspinatus weakness 4/5. ER 4/5. Neg apprehension. Distal sensation intact, radial pulse intact, grip 5/5. Neck ROM full, neg Spurling.
Urine hCG neg.

Tx:

- acetaminophen 1000 mg q8h PRN, do not exceed 3 g/day
- sling for comfort x 1 wk, gentle pendulum exercises, no overhead lifting

Work note given, pt verbalized understanding.

note:
Doctor: Welcome in. I have you down as a 22-year-old female coming in about pelvic pain. Tell me what's been happening.
Patient: It's been going on for about a year and a half. It's an aching pain low in my belly, and it gets way worse right before and during my period. Sometimes it's there even when I'm not bleeding.
Doctor: How bad is it on a scale of zero to ten?
Patient: During my period it's an eight. The rest of the month it's more like a three or four. I miss work some months.
Doctor: Does anything go along with it, like pain with sex or with bowel movements?
Patient: Yes, pain deep inside with sex, and bowel movements hurt during my period. Um, is that related?
Doctor: It can be. Any fever, unusual discharge, burning when you urinate, or blood in your stool?
Patient: No fever, no discharge, no burning, and no blood in my stool. I haven't lost weight either.
Doctor: I see you were traveling recently.
Patient: I got back from Southeast Asia about three weeks ago. I had diarrhea for a couple of days there, but it went away on its own. I'm worried I picked something up.
Doctor: That sounds like it cleared, and it wouldn't explain pain going back a year and a half. What have you been taking for the pain?
Patient: Ibuprofen 400 milligrams, maybe three times a day during my period. It only helps a little.
Doctor: Any other medications or allergies?
Patient: No other medications and no allergies.
Doctor: Okay. Your blood pressure today was 112 over 70, heart rate 72, temperature 98.2. On exam your belly is soft, but you are tender deep in the pelvis behind the cervix, and I feel some firmness along the ligaments there. Your urine pregnancy test was negative, and the chlamydia and gonorrhea swabs I sent last week were negative too.
Patient: So what do you think it is?
Doctor: My impression is chronic pelvic pain, and given the cyclic pattern, the deep pain with sex, and the exam, I suspect endometriosis. The diarrhea from your trip has resolved, so I don't think it is part of this. Let's stop the ibuprofen and start naproxen 500 milligrams twice a day with food during your period. I also want to start norethindrone acetate 5 milligrams once a day to calm things down. I'm ordering a transvaginal ultrasound, and if the pain isn't much better in three months we can talk about laparoscopy.
Patient: Will the pill have side effects?
Doctor: Some spotting or nausea is common. Come back in six weeks, and call sooner for fever, heavy bleeding, or severe pain.
Patient: Okay, that makes sense.
summary: A 22-year-old female returned from Southeast Asia three weeks ago and has had 18 months of cyclic pelvic pain, worse around periods, with deep pain during sex and painful bowel movements during menses. She denies fever, discharge, burning with urination, blood in the stool and weight loss, and a brief traveler's diarrhea has resolved. Exam showed deep pelvic tenderness behind the cervix with firmness along the ligaments, and the urine pregnancy test and chlamydia and gonorrhea swabs were negative. The impression is chronic pelvic pain with suspected endometriosis. Ibuprofen is stopped, naproxen and norethindrone acetate are started, a transvaginal ultrasound is ordered, and she returns in six weeks.

note:
Telehealth video visit with an 81-year-old female who has a right ankle injury. She rolled her ankle inward two days ago while stepping off a curb and has had outer ankle pain and swelling since. She was able to take several steps right after it happened but now walks with a limp. She denies hearing a pop at the time of the injury, denies numbness or tingling in the foot, and denies pain in the knee or lower leg. She has hypertension, which is well controlled on lisinopril 10 mg daily, and she has no known drug allergies. She has been using ice and elevation at home.

She reports a home blood pressure of 128/76 and a pulse of 72. On the video exam there is mild swelling and light bruising over the outer ankle with no visible deformity. She can wiggle all of her toes and move the foot up and down. She is able to take four steps with her cane with a mild limp. When she presses on the area herself, she is tender just in front of and below the outer ankle bone, with no tenderness over the back of the ankle bone or at the base of the small toe side of the foot.

My impression is a lateral ankle sprain. Based on her ability to bear weight and the location of tenderness, a fracture is unlikely and an X-ray is not needed right now. Plan is acetaminophen 500 mg every six hours as needed for pain. I advised her to avoid ibuprofen because of her age and her blood pressure medicine. She will continue ice and elevation, use a lace-up ankle brace, and keep walking with her cane. I showed her gentle ankle motion exercises to start in three days. I will order an ankle X-ray if she is not clearly better at a follow-up video visit in two weeks, and she should go to clinic sooner if she cannot bear weight or develops numbness.

She denies a pop, numbness, tingling and pain in the knee or lower leg. On video she had mild swelling and bruising, could move her toes and foot, and walked four steps with a cane, with tenderness only in front of and below the outer ankle bone. The impression is a lateral ankle sprain with a fracture unlikely. Acetaminophen as needed, ice, elevation, a lace-up brace, her cane and gentle exercises are advised, with a video follow-up in two weeks.

note:
Telehealth video visit with an 88-year-old male with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis who reports new symptoms over the past five days. He joined from home by video with his daughter helping with the tablet. He has numbness and weakness of the left leg that began about five days ago and is slowly getting worse. His left foot drags when he walks and he had one near fall in the bathroom, with no injury. He denies fever, denies burning with urination, denies new cough, and denies blurred vision. He has not noticed any new problems with his arms or his speech. A urinalysis at his primary care office last week was normal, according to him and his daughter.

He stopped his dimethyl fumarate 240 mg twice daily about three months ago because the copay became more than he can afford, and he did not tell our clinic. He also takes amlodipine 5 mg daily for hypertension. He has no known drug allergies.

Home measurements today are blood pressure 134/78, pulse 70, and temperature 98.1 on his home thermometer. On the video exam he is alert, his speech is clear and fluent, and his face moves symmetrically. He holds both arms out without drift. When he stands with his walker, he lifts the left leg noticeably less than the right, and a left foot drop is visible when he takes a few steps.

My impression is a multiple sclerosis relapse involving the left leg, likely related to being off disease modifying therapy for three months. By history and the recent urinalysis there are no signs of infection. His hypertension has been stable. We also have medication non-adherence because of cost.

Plan is to start prednisone 60 mg daily for five days, taken in the morning with food, and to have him check his blood pressure each day while on it. I am ordering an MRI of the brain and cervical spine with and without contrast within the next week. I am referring him to social work and our pharmacy assistance program to arrange copay help, and he will restart dimethyl fumarate 240 mg twice daily once that is in place. Home physical therapy for leg strengthening and fall precautions were discussed. He will have a follow-up video visit in two weeks. He should go to the emergency department for fever, vision loss, inability to walk, or new weakness in an arm.
summary: An 88-year-old male with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis and hypertension had a telehealth video visit for five days of worsening left leg numbness and weakness with a dragging left foot and one near fall. He denies fever, burning with urination, new cough and blurred vision, and a recent urinalysis was normal. He stopped dimethyl fumarate about three months ago because of cost, and the video exam showed reduced left leg lift and a visible left foot drop. The impression is a multiple sclerosis relapse likely related to being off therapy, along with cost-related non-adherence. Prednisone is started, an MRI is ordered, social work and pharmacy assistance are arranged, and follow-up is in two weeks.

soap.subjective: 88-year-old male with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, joining from home by video with his daughter helping. Numbness and weakness of the left leg for about five days, slowly worsening, with a dragging left foot and one near fall in the bathroom without injury. Denies fever, burning with urination, new cough and blurred vision, and has not noticed new problems with his arms or speech. A urinalysis at his primary care office last week was normal by report. Stopped dimethyl fumarate 240 mg twice daily about three months ago because the copay was unaffordable and did not tell the clinic. Also takes amlodipine 5 mg daily for hypertension. No known drug allergies.
soap.objective: Home measurements: blood pressure 134/78, pulse 70, temperature 98.1 on a home thermometer. Video exam: alert, speech clear and fluent, face moves symmetrically, holds both arms out without drift. Standing with a walker he lifts the left leg noticeably less than the right, and a left foot drop is visible on a few steps. Urinalysis last week normal by report.
soap.assessment: Multiple sclerosis relapse involving the left leg, likely related to three months off disease modifying therapy. No signs of infection by history and recent urinalysis. Hypertension stable. Medication non-adherence because of cost.
plan: Start prednisone 60 mg daily for five days in the morning with food, with daily blood pressure checks
MRI of the brain and cervical spine with and without contrast within the next week
Refer to social work and the pharmacy assistance program for copay help
Restart dimethyl fumarate 240 mg twice daily once assistance is in place
Home physical therapy for leg strengthening and fall precautions
Follow-up video visit in two weeks
Go to the emergency department for fever, vision loss, inability to walk or new weakness in an arm
